title: The Price of Admission
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 41 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
Greg Universe announced that the benefit concert would be free.

He announced it while holding a sheet of paper that said the sound equipment alone would cost more than we had.

“Okay,” I said. “How free?”

He gave me the smile that meant he hoped I would forget to look at the numbers.

“Free free.”

“That's a very expensive type of free.”

“Come on, Jasper. It's for the lantern repairs. People shouldn't have to pay to help.”

“Agreed. The electrician would also like to eat.”

Greg looked at the paper.

Then at me.

“That's a fair point.”

It was a bright morning at Starwake Pier. The boards smelled of salt and the faint sweetness of somebody's breakfast pastries. The little stage at the end had hosted three open-mic nights, one birthday party, and an argument about whether Toph was legally allowed to call a drum solo a structural failure.

She had won the argument.

I was beginning to suspect she won most arguments through a combination of accuracy and refusing to get bored.

Greg sat on the stage edge with his guitar across his knees.

“What if we ask people to donate?” he said.

“We can.”

“Then they'll donate.”

“Some will.”

“Is that your gentle way of telling me I don't have a budget?”

“It's my direct way of telling you that you have three budgets and none of them agree.”

He laughed, but it ended quickly. I knew that sound now. He was embarrassed by something he had hoped would feel generous.

I sat beside him and laid the paper between us.

“We can make it free to attend and still make the costs visible. People can donate if they're able. We can ask the kitchen whether they'll contribute food. We can pay the electrician.”

“It's just a small stage.”

“Electricity is still electricity on a small stage.”

“Hey, I know a guy.”

“I know you know a guy. I want to know whether the guy knows he's working.”

Greg put a hand to his chest.

“Harsh.”

“Accurate.”

“Also harsh.”

We began with the actual costs. Cables. Temporary lights. Replacement anchors for the threshold lamps. Weather covers. Materials for the footpaths. Chairs. A ramp adjustment, because the stage entrance had a lip that made the word *accessible* optimistic at best.

Greg looked up when I pointed to the ramp.

“That's been there since the first show.”

“I know.”

“I should've fixed it.”

“Then we fix it.”

He stared at the page.

“Sometimes I get so excited about the song I forget somebody has to build the room around it.”

“That's why bands have crew.”

“Sometimes the crew is also the bass player.”

“Then the bass player deserves a break.”

That earned a real laugh.

We took our list to Lanternwell Square. Neri was hunched over a table, trying to flatten a map that had been soaked in Threadrain. The paper lifted whenever they moved a hand, which made them look as though they were playing a deeply uncooperative game.

“We're planning a concert,” Greg announced.

“Of course you are,” Neri said. “How can I help?”

“You can tell us what needs fixing most,” I said.

Neri handed over a list.

It was longer than the stage.

Greg whistled.

“I was thinking maybe a couple of lantern brackets.”

“That's how it started,” Neri said. “Then a stair was damaged. Then an archive label went missing. Then the Brasswatch Door settled into the ground by half an inch. Nothing catastrophic, but it adds up.”

“It usually does,” I said.

Greg read down the list. “We can't pay for all of this with one show.”

“No,” Neri replied. “You don't have to.”

That was the first thing anyone had said all morning that made Greg look relieved.

We divided the work into projects people could actually see. One concert might buy a length of copper wire, a bag of fasteners, and new waterproof covers for the lamps. Somebody else could volunteer a repair shift. A neighbor could donate leftover timber. Nobody would be asked to disclose why they needed a particular door open.

On the way back to the pier, Greg bought us two pastries and tried to pretend the price had not hurt his feelings.

“You're very quiet,” I said.

“Thinking.”

“Dangerous.”

“Historically.”

He offered me the bigger pastry. I took it without comment.

“It's not that I don't want to help,” he said. “I just keep making the big promise before I figure out whether I can keep it.”

I thought of all the songs he'd written when there had been nobody to ask for help.

“I know.”

“You make it look easy.”

“No. I make a list. That's different.”

He smiled at that.

At the pier we found Danse examining a box of wiring supplies with the expression of a man considering whether to arrest the contents.

Greg waved.

“Hey! Perfect timing. You know anything about stage lights?”

“I know enough to ask why you've connected three mismatched adapters.”

Greg winced.

“Creative freedom?”

“Electrical hazard.”

“Less inspiring.”

Danse took the adapters apart with an economy of movement that reminded me of somebody opening a particularly frustrating jar. Greg listened as he explained the problem. I watched them for a moment and felt pleased that I did not need to translate every conversation between people I knew.

At one point Greg offered to play him something while he worked.

“I don't require entertainment,” Danse said.

“No charge.”

Danse gave him a suspicious look.

“Fine.”

Greg began a soft progression on the guitar. It was not a song yet. Just a few chords circling an idea.

Danse kept working.

After a minute he said, “The second phrase is stronger than the first.”

Greg stopped.

“You were listening?”

“I have ears.”

“Yeah, but you have *opinions*. That's the good stuff.”

Danse looked increasingly alarmed by the possibility that he had accidentally become a musical collaborator.

I excused myself before I laughed in front of both of them.

By sunset the budget finally balanced. Not because we'd discovered a fortune, but because the concert had become a real community project with people agreeing to specific jobs.

Greg walked me to the far end of the pier, where the railing caught the last warmth of the day.

“You still want to be seen with the guy who nearly electrocuted a charity concert?” he asked.

“You didn't nearly electrocute it.”

“Danse says otherwise.”

“Danse thinks exposed wires are a personal insult.”

“They kind of are.”

I turned toward him.

“Greg.”

“Yeah?”

“I like you when you're excited. I like you when you're worried. I like you when you ask for help instead of pretending the whole world is your guitar case to carry.”

His smile softened.

“Even when I'm awkward?”

“Especially then. It's one of your finest talents.”

He laughed and brushed a strand of hair away from my face. His fingers paused beside my cheek, waiting. I leaned into his hand.

“Can I kiss you?” he asked.

“You can.”

He did, slowly, with the sea wind tugging at his shirt and his guitar strap still crooked over one shoulder. The kiss tasted faintly of cinnamon from the pastry we'd shared. When we drew apart, his forehead rested against mine.

“You know I don't need you at every rehearsal,” he said.

“I know.”

“But I do want to know when you'll be around.”

“Then I'll tell you. We made that agreement for a reason.”

He nodded. We both knew the difference between a calendar and a claim on a person's every hour. It had taken real conversations to learn it.

“I've got one more question,” he said.

“About the budget?”

“Nope.”

“Good. I've run out of numbers.”

He grinned. “Dance with me?”

“There's no music.”

He tapped the rhythm of a slow song against the railing.

“There is now.”

I took his hand.

We danced in the narrow space between the stage and the water, badly and happily, while the last workers packed away tools. Later we went home. I put the cost sheet on the counter, Greg set his guitar beside the door, and the rest of the evening belonged to the two of us.

The next morning, a fresh notice appeared at Lanternwell Square:

FREE CONCERT — OPTIONAL DONATIONS — EVERYONE WELCOME.

Below it, in Greg's loopy handwriting, he'd added:

WE PAY THE ELECTRICIAN.

I smiled until I noticed the paper beneath the notice.

Someone had copied the list of needed repairs twice.

The names were different. The requests were the same.

I tore off the duplicate and took both pages to Neri.

The concert would still happen.

But before we collected a single copper, we needed to know which repairs actually existed.
